newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistanis fire in air to celebrate Bhutto ouster.
newsitem.headline: Pakistanis fire in air to celebrate Bhutto ouster.

text.p: Joyous Pakistanis fired guns in the air on Tuesday to celebrate the dismissal of prime minister Benazir Bhutto, as the military kept a low profile during an abrupt transfer of power.
Pakistan greeted the fourth dismissal of a government in eight years with scattered celebrations and few regrets for Bhutto's three-year rule.
"We are so happy because the government was corrupt," Ishtiaq Khattak, a 23-year-old student in the Pakistani capital, said. "Today is a very happy day for the Pakistan nation."
While peaceful and without bloodshed, the transfer of power to caretaker Prime Minister Meraj Khalid was tinged with apprehension, at least in the opening hours.

Under the cover of darkness, army troops took over sensitive spots including state television and radio. The mobile phone network was cut in the capital Islamabad and telephone lines to the homes of sacked federal ministers were out of action.
Bhutto was kept under wraps in her official residence at the edge of a sprawl of imposing government buildings. Troops turned back former ministers who tried to visit her.

But the military, which has ruled Pakistan for 24 of its 49 years since independence but stayed out of direct power since 1988, remained in the shadows. Only small numbers of soldiers could be glimpsed at key installations.
Shops and businesses were open as usual.
In Islamabad, activists of the opposition Pakistan Muslim League slit the throat of a goat in an Islamic gesture of thanksgiving.

Residents of the northern town of Peshawar, gateway to war-scarred Afghanistan, were awakened at dawn by gunfire celebrating news of Bhutto's ouster. Elated residents covered streets with rose petals.
In Rawalpindi near Islamabad, about 200 opposition party supporters fired assault rifles into the air and hoisted a traffic policeman on to their shoulders in joy.

In the southern city of Karachi, hundreds of Mohajir National Movement (MQM) workers gathered at party headquarters to cheer and dance. Elsewhere in the commercial and financial capital jubilant youths destroyed police barricades.
Karachi shops ran out of sweets, residents said.
The Karachi stock exchange was closed for a scheduled holiday but investors did brisk kerb trade in its parking lot, with favoured scrips posting substantial gains, dealers said.
In Lahore, capital of Punjab province, people fired shots in the air and swapped sweets.
Hundreds of activists from the Islamic Jamaat-i-Islami party held a celebration march in Islamabad, chanting slogans against the ousted government.
At Aabpara, Islamabad's oldest market and the focal point of a demonstration last week against Bhutto's government, residents were overjoyed.
"There have been lots of price hikes and unemployment and industries have been shut," said Mohammad Azin, a 65-year-old retired government accountant.
Residents hailed President Farooq Leghari, who issued the order removing Bhutto, his one-time Pakistan People's Party ally.
"No one was expecting this from him as he was a party worker," said the white-bearded Azin. "This step proves that what he did is for the larger benefit of the nation."
